title: The Inventory of the family house on Kessler Street
premise: After her mother's funeral, Astrid Whitlock returns to the family house on Kessler Street to sort its contents, keeping a meticulous written inventory that becomes a ledger of everything her mother never said. Buried in the basement she finds reel-to-reel tapes and photographs revealing her mother once wrote songs, performed under another name, and loved a woman named June—choosing silence over scandal in 1960s Ohio. As Astrid plays the tapes, she must decide whether to preserve the house as a shrine or let the truth out, all while her own marriage quietly frays under the same inherited habit of concealment. The novel ends with Astrid recording herself singing one of the unfinished songs and mailing it to June's surviving daughter, choosing disclosure—and love—over the safety of invisibility.
about_author: Paloma Okafor is a former archivist who spent six years cataloging unclaimed estate collections in the American Midwest. Her fiction explores what families keep, discard, and refuse to name.

chapters.title: Everything Must Be Counted
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Nine days after the funeral, Astrid begins an inventory of the Kessler Street house with a legal pad and her mother's fountain pen, itemizing objects while avoiding rooms. Her husband Daniel calls from Chicago; their conversation is polite and hollow. Emotional beat: grief displaced into control—the inventory as armor against feeling.

chapters.title: The Room That Wasn't on the List
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She finally opens the locked basement door and finds a reel-to-reel recorder, stacks of unlabeled tapes, and a shoebox of photographs showing a young woman at a microphone—a woman who is unmistakably her mother. Emotional beat: the first crack in the official version of her mother's life.

chapters.title: Side A
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, intercut with tape recordings of her mother's voice, younger and warmer than Astrid ever knew it. The songs are good—startlingly good—and one is addressed to someone named J. Emotional beat: wonder curdling into betrayal; the mother she mourned is now a stranger.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Photographs
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She tracks down a name: June Calloway, listed in an old club program from 1963. A call to a retired bartender yields fragments—two women, one guitar, a sudden disappearance. Meanwhile Daniel announces he wants to sell the house quickly. Emotional beat: investigation as avoidance of her own unraveling marriage.

chapters.title: What Survival Cost
chapters.summary: Aunt Ruthie's POV. Visiting her aunt, Astrid hears the era's terms plainly: a Black woman writing love songs for another woman in 1960s Dayton could lose everything. Ruthie defends the silence as protection, not cowardice. Emotional beat: sympathy complicates anger—Astrid sees the price her mother paid to survive.

chapters.title: The Unrecorded Song
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. On the drive home, a late-night radio program plays a song Astrid recognizes from the tapes—but this version has lyrics the recordings never contained, credited to 'J. Calloway.' Someone is still alive, still singing. Emotional beat: urgency ignites; the past is not closed, and time is running out.

chapters.title: Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She abandons the object inventory and starts a second list: every silence, every deflection, every question never asked. Daniel arrives unannounced and finds her weeping over the tapes; they have the fight ten years deferred. Emotional beat: climax of the marriage thread—she realizes she has become her mother.

chapters.title: June
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Astrid traveling to find June Calloway, now ninety-one, in a care home outside Columbus; and June's memory of 1964, the last night she and Astrid's mother played together before fear separated them. Emotional beat: two inheritances meet—June gives Astrid the missing verse of the unrecorded song.

chapters.title: The Last Item
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Back at Kessler Street, she finds her mother's final letter, unsent, tucked inside the piano bench—an apology thirty years late, asking forgiveness for choosing safety. Astrid records herself singing the completed song, voice cracking, and mails the tape to June's daughter. Emotional beat: catharsis; the inventory ends with one entry—'one song, delivered.'

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, months later. The house is sold; the tapes are archived at a university collection under both women's names. At a small memorial concert, June's daughter performs the recovered songs while Astrid listens beside Daniel—not saved, but honest now. Emotional beat: resolution without repair; inheritance transformed from silence into song.
